parsed_answer.content:
To understand the architecture of modern enterprise Java, one must distinguish clearly between the Spring Framework and Spring Boot, two distinct yet deeply symbiotic technologies. The Spring Framework is a comprehensive, foundational programming and configuration model for modern Java-based enterprise applications. It provides core infrastructure support through Inversion of Control (IoC), Dependency Injection (DI), transaction management, AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming), and dedicated modules for web applications, data access, and messaging. However, raw Spring requires exhaustive boilerplate configuration: developers must explicitly declare ContextLoaders, DispatcherServlets, view resolvers, database connection pools, and third-party dependency versions in bloated XML files or complex `@Configuration` classes, carefully managing classpath conflicts and transitive dependency versions.

Spring Boot sits on top of Spring as an opinionated meta-framework designed to eliminate this setup friction. It does not replace the Spring Framework; rather, it supercharges it by introducing three core pillars: Auto-Configuration, Starters, and Actuator. Spring Boot auto-configures your application based on the jar dependencies present on the classpath (e.g., if H2 and Spring Data JPA are detected, it automatically spins up an embedded datasource and entity manager). Spring Boot Starters curate curated transitive dependency descriptors (like `spring-boot-starter-web`) so developers never have to guess version compatibility matrices again. By packaging applications into self-contained executable JAR files containing embedded web servers (like Tomcat or Undertow), Spring Boot radically simplifies packaging, deployment, and cloud-native scaling.

rows: Manual XML or Java-based @Configuration for beans, dispatchers, and datasources.
Auto-configured based on classpath heuristics via @EnableAutoConfiguration.
Manual tracking of transitive dependencies and compatible library versions.
Curated 'Starter' POMs that enforce tested version parity across ecosystems.
Typically packaged as a WAR file deployed to an external Servlet container.
Packaged as an executable fat JAR with an embedded web server (Tomcat/Jetty).
Manual integration of JMX, custom health checks, and logging configurations.
Spring Boot Actuator out-of-the-box health endpoints, metrics, and thread dumps.

items: Auto-configuration operates at startup by evaluating `Condition` evaluations (such as `@ConditionalOnClass` or `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`), inspecting the JVM classpath to dynamically register necessary infrastructure beans before the ApplicationContext refreshes.

Spring Boot's fat JAR architecture repackages application classes and all nested dependency jars inside a custom archive layout (`BOOT-INF/classes` and `BOOT-INF/lib`), executed via a specialized Launcher class that bootstraps a custom URL classloader.

Starters leverage Maven and Gradle Bill of Materials (BOM) imports to pin framework dependencies to versions that have undergone exhaustive regression testing by the Spring engineering team, eliminating runtime ClassNotFound exceptions caused by version skew.

parsed_answer.content: A common production trap for junior developers is blindly relying on Spring Boot auto-configuration without understanding the underlying Spring beans being instantiated. When troubleshooting bean override issues or diagnosing unexpected transaction proxies, use `--debug` when launching your JAR to print the Conditions Evaluation Report, which explicitly logs why specific auto-configurations were matched or skipped.
